base.description: Base rig setup with mast centered laterally (upper shroud lengths adjusted until jib-halyard-to-sheer measurements match port/starboard). Upper shroud tension set to 22 and lower shroud tension set to 12 on a Loos PT-2 gauge. Headstay pulled taut down the front face of the mast; measured from a mark level with the top of the white band near the gooseneck down to the center of the bottom headstay pin (including toggles): 54 1/2 in. Guide covers three separate tension charts (Southern Spars mast w/ M2 or J2 mainsail, Selden mast, and SD-1 mainsail on any mast); the Southern Spars M2/J2 chart is transcribed below as the primary table.
base.notes: Headstay length measured taut: 54 1/2 in (guide's own unit is inches, not converted). Pre-bend (aft bend, measured from back of mast track to front of main halyard at the spreaders) should be 1 1/2 - 2 1/2 in; SD-1 main favors closer to 1 1/2 in, M2 main favors closer to 2 1/2 in. Selden-mast and SD-1-sail tension charts in the source give different base numbers (e.g. Selden uppers/lowers turns-from-base and a 1385 mm forestay reading at the base 8-10kt band; SD-1 base is 18/8 on PT-2) and are not transcribed into these bands.

downwind.notes: Spinnaker set out the main hatch, between shrouds and mast, to keep clear of the water while hoisting. Tack pulled tight to end of fully extended bowsprit; before planning/deeper sailing the tack can be eased 4-6 in to help the sail rotate to windward. Inside gybe (spinnaker passed between its own luff and the headstay) is the standard technique. Three douse types used depending on approach: windward douse (port-tack approach to a port mark or starboard-tack approach to a starboard mark), leeward douse (starboard-tack approach to a starboard mark), and gybe/"Mexican" douse (starboard-tack approach to a port mark without room to complete the gybe first).

verbatimNotes: At max upwind trim, mainsail leech telltales at the top of the main should be stalling 25-30% of the time; in light wind or when building speed they should be flowing 80-100% of the time.

Jib leech telltales (upper leech) should be flowing when the jib is trimmed properly for upwind; in 10+ kt flat water the jib leech can sheet to the inside 18 in spreader mark while the telltale still flows, while light/lumpy conditions favor the outside 22 in spreader mark.

Jib halyard: more tension = flatter sail, less tension = deeper sail. In light air, small wrinkles ~4-8 in aft of the luff are the target; as wind builds, tighten just to the point the wrinkles disappear.
Jib lead car forward = tighter leech/rounder foot; aft = open leech/flatter foot. In-hauler: more = tighter leech/rounder foot; less = open leech/flatter foot.
Mainsail lowest batten should hook slightly to windward of the boom when the mainsheet is trimmed properly (indicator of correct outhaul tension).
